title: Active Investigation in Mills, Change of Plans for Students Dropped at Freden Park - NewsBreak
text:
By Kolby Fedore ,
6 hours ago
Due to an active and ongoing law enforcement situation in the area of Badger Lane in Mills, all NCSD students whose regular after-school bus stop is Freden Park will be transported from their home school to the NCSD Bus Hub, where they will be held until a parent or guardian can pick them up. This per a news release from the Natrona County School District.
Details for Freden Park Bus Riders:
Students who are normally dropped off at Freden Park will be held at the NCSD Bus Hub with active supervision until a parent/guardian can be reached for an alternate pick up.
Students will only be released to a parent or guardian.
NCSD Bus Hub is located at 136 W. 8th Street.
Parents/guardians, please contact NCSD Transportation at 307-253-5280 with any questions.
This notice is only for NCSD Bus Riders whose bus stop is located at Freden Park.
All other bus routes will occur as normal.
Badger Lane is currently closed from Pontiac Street to River Crossing. Please avoid the area at this time.
Rockers We've Lost in 2025 There's some amazing talent that's no longer with us, but what a legacy they left behind. Gallery Credit: Chad Childers, Loudwire Larry Busacca, Getty Images Ozzy Osbourne (Black Sabbath) Ozzy Osbourne , 17 days removed from playing his final performance at the Back to the Beginning concert marking his and Black Sabbath 's last show, died on July 22 at the age of 76 .
"It is with more sadness than mere words can convey that we have to report that our beloved Ozzy Osbourne has passed away this morning. He was with his family and surrounded by love," shared a statement from the Osbourne family.
As a member of Black Sabbath, Ozzy and his cohorts are frequently considered the pioneers of heavy metal music.
Albums like their self-titled debut and Paranoid , both released in 1970, helped redefine a disillusioned new decade.
"We were just doing the opposite of what was happening at the time," Osbourne later recalled . "All that love stuff of the late '60s made me sick. We wanted to get to the dark side of life."
Later dubbed the "Prince of Darkness," Osbourne helped shape the band’s sound and style in the '70s before being fired in 1979 after a couple of underperforming albums. "None of us wanted to drag this black-magic shit around forever so we tried to get a bit modern – but you should stick to what you know best," Osbourne told the Guardian in 2011. "The thing was, at that time, I had nothing to lose. If I even got to make a new record and it was a flop, who cared?"
Osbourne shot out of the gate with a pair of smash solo albums featuring the late guitarist Randy Rhoads : 1980's Blizzard of Ozz and 1981's Diary of a Madman . He eventually moved away from the "black magic shit," scoring far more mainstream hits with songs like "Shot in the Dark," “No More Tears” and "Mama, I'm Coming Home."
In 1996, Osbourne curated his first Ozzfest , a music and lifestyle festival built around established and up-and-coming metal and hard rock acts. The festival became an annual event, then a well-received tour which even ventured overseas.
Arguably the most unexpected turn of his career came in 2002 as Ozzy became a reality TV star. The Osbournes followed Ozzy and his family – wife, Sharon, daughter, Kelly and son, Jack – through the antics of their daily lives. The show was an instant hit for MTV, becoming the most viewed program on the network. Ozzy was introduced to a new generation of fans, while his family launched their own separate careers.
Osbourne continued to fluctuate between periods of sobriety and drug use before finally getting clean. In 2018, Osbourne admitted that he had found peace . “How did I think going into a bar and getting smashed and doing all that cocaine was fun?," he wondered. "Right now, you had a gun, a bag of cocaine and a gallon of booze and you said, ‘Take your pick,’ I’d pick up the gun. It’s not worth it."
He courted controversy by peeing near the Alamo , a historical shrine in Texas, and famously bit off the head of a bat. Osbourne later apologized for urinating, but only after a lengthy period in which he was banned from performing in the area. He also explained the incident with the bat, claiming that he thought it was fake.
Yet, none of this ultimately overshadowed his contributions to music. Long after all of those tabloid headlines yellow and fade, Osbourne will be remembered as a three-time Grammy winner, a member of both the Rock and Roll and U.K. Music halls of fame, and as a co-creator of heavy metal. Barry Brecheisen, Getty Images Brent Hinds (ex-Mastodon) It was revealed that former Mastodon guitarist Brent Hinds died on Aug. 20 at the age of 51 after being involved in a motorcycle accident in Atlanta.
"We are in a state of unfathomable sadness and grief," shared the band members in their initial statement after learning of Hinds' passing. "We are heartbroken, shocked, and still trying to process the loss of this creative force with whom we’ve shared so many triumphs, milestones and the creation of music that has touched the hearts of so many. Our hearts are with Brent’s family, friends and fans."
Hinds formed Mastodon in 2000 alongside bassist/vocalist Troy Sanders , guitarist Bill Kelliher and drummer/vocalist Brann Dailor . The lineup remained intact for 25 years and released some of the most acclaimed progressive metal albums of the 21st century, including Leviathan , Blood Mountain and Crack the Skye . Mastodon announced Hinds' departure in March 2025.
In addition to Mastodon, Hinds was playing with Fiend Without a Face, West End Motel and Dirty B & the Boys at the time of his death and had also performed with Four Hour Fogger, The Last of the Blue Eyed Devils, Giraffe Tongue Orchestra and Legend of the Seagullmen previously as well.
Alberto E. Rodriguez, Getty Images Garth Hudson (The Band) Garth Hudson, the legendary keyboardist, organist and saxophonist for The Band , died on Jan. 21 at the age of 87.
Hudson was the last living member of the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame band. He passed away peacefully in his sleep after a lengthy illness.
Prior to The Band, Hudson had also played with Levon Helm in Ronnie Hawkins' supporting group The Hawks.
Hudson's work with The Band has yielded recognition from the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, the Canadian Music Hall of Fame, a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award and induction into Canada's Walk of Fame. Pete Cronin, Getty Images John Sykes (Thin Lizzy, Whitesnake, Blue Murder) John Sykes , the former guitarist for Thin Lizzy and Whitesnake , died on Jan. 20 at the age of 65.
An official statement confirmed that Sykes had been diagnosed with cancer.
"He will be remembered by many as a man with exceptional musical talent but for those who didn't know him personally, he was a thoughtful, kind and charismatic man whose presence lit up the room," according to the statement. "He certainly marched to the beat of his own drum and always pulled for the underdog."
Sykes appeared on Thin Lizzy's harder-edged 1983 album Thunder and Lightning , the group's Top 5 U.K. hit studio finale with the late frontman Phil Lynott . Sykes then joined Whitesnake for a two-album mid-'80s stint that began with the reworked 1984 edition of Slide It In .
He co-wrote all but two songs on 1987's eight-times platinum international Top 10 hit Whitesnake , including the No. 2 U.S. smash " Is This Love ." But unfortunately, his relationship with singer David Coverdale was strained from the beginning.
"John was and is an incredible talent," Coverdale later argued. "Our musical chemistry was great, but it didn’t work personally. The truth of the matter is no matter how incredible of an album that we made together, we were unable to connect as people."
Sykes other credits include work with Tygers of Pan Tang and Blue Murder. Central Press/Hulton Archive, Getty Images Marianne Faithfull The '60s era folk singer Marianne Faithfull died on Jan. 30 at the age of 78.
Her biggest hit, "As Tears Go By," was co-written by Mick Jagger, Keith Richards and Andrew Loog Oldham. The singer also had a highly publicized relationship with Jagger between 1966 and 1970.
Her music career also featured such standout tracks as "Come and Stay With Me," "This Little Bird" and "Summer Nights." In latter years, she would make guest appearances on Metallica's "The Memory Remains" and star in the corresponding video.
Faithfull also balanced an acting career that included roles in the films I'll Never Forget What'sisname , The Girl on a Motorcycle, Hamlet and Ghost Story . She also was featured i several theatrical productions including Three Sisters, Early Morning, Alice in Wonderland and Hamlet . YouTube: Produce Like a Pro Dave Jerden (Producer) The legendary music producer Dave Jerden died on Feb. 5 at the age of 75.
His career covered many of the behind the scenes studio details on major albums, ranging from producing to serving as an audio engineer and a mixer.
Among his credits are work on Talking Heads' Remain in Light , Herbie Hancock's Future Shock, The Rolling Stones' Dirty Work , Jane's Addiction's Nothing's Shocking and Ritual de lo Habitual, Social Distortion's self-titled album, Alice in Chains' Facelift and Dirt albums, Anthrax's Sound of White Noise, The Offspring's Ixnay on the Hombre and Americana albums and plenty more. Roberta Bayley/Redferns, Getty Images David Johansen (New York Dolls, Buster Poindexter) David Johansen died from cancer on Feb. 28 at the age of 75.
Johansen first came to fame in the '70s as the leader of the influential proto-punk outfit The New York Dolls. The group would issue five albums total, though most of the acclaim comes from their two 1970s records, New York Dolls and Too Much Too Soon .
After the band split, Johansen issued four solo album before reinventing himself with the lounge-y persona Buster Poindexter where he then saw a career resurgence with four more studio albums.
In addition to his music work, Johansen also carved out a solid acting career which included memorable turns in the Bill Murray holiday film Scrooged and the Richard Dreyfuss-starring film Let It Ride . Other credits include the movies Freejack and Tales From the Darkside .
Jonathan Leibson, Getty Images Clem Burke (Blondie) Legendary Rock and Roll Hall of Fame drummer Clem Burke of Blondie died on April 6 at the age of 70.
A statement released following his passing revealed that Burke had died "following a private battle with cancer."
“Clem was not just a drummer; he was the heartbeat of Blondie,” the band added. “His talent, energy, and passion for music were unmatched, and his contributions to our sound and success are immeasurable. Beyond his musicianship, Clem was a source of inspiration both on and off the stage. His vibrant spirit, infectious enthusiasm and rock solid work ethic touched everyone who had the privilege of knowing him," said the group in a statement.
Burke joined the band in 1975 and was part of every one of Blondie's albums alongside Debbie Harry and Chris Stein.
After Blondie split, Burke spent time as a session musician playing on recordings for Eurythmics, Iggy Pop, Joan Jett and Pete Townshend in the '80s. He also spent time playing with the bands Dramarama and The Romantics and subbed in briefly for Ramones during a lineup change in the group.
Fin Costello/Redferns, Getty Images / Theo Wargo, Getty Images Judas Priest, Les Binks Les Binks, the onetime drummer of Judas Priest , died on April 15 at the age of 77.
Binks was a key figure in the early years of Judas Priest, having joined the group in 1977 for their tour in support of the Sin After Sin album. He remained with the group through 1979 and appeared on Stained Class and Killing Machine albums as well.
Binks left the band during the touring of the Killing Machine album and would later resurface in 1981 with the band Lionheart. The drummer's credits also include the bands Tytan, Raw Glory, Broken Bones and Kindred Spirit.
The drummer was inducted with Judas Priest when they went into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Fryderyk Gabowicz, Getty Images Mike Peters (The Alarm) Mike Peters, longtime frontman for The Alarm , died on April 29 at the age of 66.
In the '80s, the band found a following at college rock radio stations thanks such standout songs as "Sixty-Eight Guns," "Strength," "Spirit of '76," "Rain in the Summertime" and "Sold Me Down the River." The band issued five studio albums with I.R.S. before Peters exited the group following promotion of their Raw album.
Peters would eventually resume his recording career under the moniker The Alarm MM++. He would continue to be a rather prolific musician issuing 16 albums from 2002 moving forward.
The singer faced health issues through much of his life. He was first diagnosed with lymphoma in 1995, but resumed his career a year later after his recovery from treatment.
In 2005, it was revealed that he had been dealing with chronic lymphocytic leukemia. It was during this period in which he founded the Love Strength Hope foundation, taken from the lyrics of one of The Alarm's biggest hits. After his recovery, he led a group of musicians and cancer survivors on a 14-day trek climbing to base camp of Mount Everest to raise awareness for cancer research. Throughout his career, he's remained a tireless campaigner advocating for bone marrow donation to save the lives of others.
In 2022, it was announced that Peters' chronic lymphocytic leukemia had returned and in 2024 he was revealed to have been in remission from treatment for Richter's Syndrome.
Michael Putland, Getty Images Rick Derringer Guitarist, songwriter and producer Rick Derringer died May 26 at the age of 77.
Derringer first came to fame performing with his brother Randy in the '60s band The McCoys. The group had their biggest success with the single "Hang On Sloopy" and scored another Top 10 hit covering the R&B favorite "Fever."
In the '70s, Derringer was part of the Edgar Winter Group while also launching his own solo career. His biggest solo hit was "Rock and Roll Hoochie Koo." In addition, he became an in-demand guitarist playing on records from Steely Dan, Alice Cooper, Bette Midler, Todd Rundgren and Barbra Streisand.
The '80s saw him utilized on hits from Air Supply, Bonnie Tyler, Meat Loaf and Cyndi Lauper. He also worked as a producer overseeing the first six studio albums of Weird Al Yankovic. His latter years saw him also touring with Peter Frampton and Ringo Starr's All-Starr Band. Central Press, Getty Images Sly Stone (Sly & the Family Stone) Sly Stone, frontman for the legendary funk-rock outfit Sly & the Family Stone, died on June 9 at the age of 82.
"It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved dad, Sly Stone of Sly and the Family Stone," a statement from his family said. "After a prolonged battle with COPD and other underlying health issues, Sly passed away peacefully, surrounded by his three children, his closest friend, and his extended family. While we mourn his absence, we take solace in knowing that his extraordinary musical legacy will continue to resonate and inspire for generations to come."
Stone worked for a time as a DJ for a radio station in San Francisco, and also landed gigs playing keyboards for acts like Dionne Warwick, the Righteous Brothers, Marvin Gaye and more prior to his founding the band.
By the second half of the '60s, he'd formed his own, multiracial band, Sly and the Family Stone, and in 1967, they released their debut album, A Whole New Thing . Though it took a couple of years, the band eventually found major success with their fourth album, Stand! , and before the decade was out, they had three Top Five singles to their name: "Everyday People," "Hot Fun in the Summertime" and "Thank You (Falettinme Be Mice Elf Agin)."
The band would split in 1975, and Stone went on to release solo music and collaborate with Funkadelic, but it's his work with Sly and the Family Stone that is most recognized.
Michael Ochs Archives, Getty Images Brian Wilson (Beach Boys) Brian Wilson, singer, songwriter and visionary of the Beach Boys, died June 11 at the age of 82.
His family shared the news on Instagram , writing, "We are heartbroken to announce that our beloved father Brian Wilson has passed away. We are at a loss for words right now. Please respect our privacy at this time as our family is grieving. We realize that we are sharing our grief with the world."
In February 2024, shortly after the death of his wife and manager, Melinda, it was announced that Wilson was suffering from dementia and that his family members had applied for conservatorship for his safety.
Along with his two younger brothers, Dennis and Carl, plus their cousin Mike Love and classmate Al Jardine, Wilson formed a band that was initially called the Pendletones. A song penned by Wilson and Love called "Surfin'" did well in Los Angeles, and at the behest of their label at the time, Candix Records, they changed their name to the Beach Boys.
And that was just the beginning. In 1962, the band was signed to Capitol Records, releasing their debut album, Surfin' Safari , during the same year. Successful album after successful album arrived after that, with Wilson not only writing songs with his bandmates but also effectively producing their albums. "They believed in me, my process, and what I was trying to achieve," Wilson said in 2016. "They didn’t know how to produce a record, so I took charge. I was a real perfectionist, and the guys respected that. But we always mixed in some humor to lighten the load."
What would later be deemed Wilson's masterpiece was released in 1966. Pet Sounds . In retrospect, Wilson would describe his purpose in making the album: "I wanted to get the vocal harmonies I love on tape," he told the Sarasota Herald-Tribune in 2016.
"It was Pet Sounds that blew me out of the water," Paul McCartney said in 1997. "I've just bought my kids each a copy of it for their education in life — I figure no one is educated musically 'til they’ve heard that album." Victor Blackman/Daily Express/Hulton Archive, Getty Images Mick Ralphs (Bad Company / Mott the Hoople) Mick Ralphs, guitarist and founding member of the classic rock bands Bad Company and Mott the Hoople, died on June 26 at the age of 81.
Paul Rodgers , his former Bad Company bandmate, shared , "Our Mick has passed, my heart just hit the ground. He has left us with exceptional songs and memories. He was my friend, my songwriting partner, an amazing and versatile guitarist who had the greatest sense of humor.
"Our last conversation a few days ago we shared a laugh but it won't be our last. There are many memories of Mick that will create laughter. Condolences to everyone who loved him especially his one true love, Susie. I will see you in heaven."
Drummer Simon Kirke also issued a statement, noting, "He was a dear friend, a wonderful songwriter and an exceptional guitarist. We will miss him deeply."
In 2016, following a tour with Bad Company, Ralphs was hospitalized with a stroke. He officially retired from performing after that.
In 1969, he helped form Mott the Hoople, remaining with the band until 1973, contributing to all of the band's studio albums in some capacity.
He also played on all of Bad Company's albums, even though he didn't always tour with them.
Sadly, Ralphs death came just months ahead of Bad Company's induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
Jason Kempin, Getty Images Bobby Sherman Bobby Sherman, the late '60s and early '70s pop-rock singer, passed away on June 24 at the age of 81. In March of 2025, the singer was diagnosed with Stage IV kidney cancer.
Sherman first started hitting the charts in 1962 and scored his biggest successes with the songs "Little Woman," "La La La (If I Had You)," "Easy Come, Easy Go," "Julie, Do Ya Love Me" and "Cried Like a Baby."
He also landed a TV role in Here Come the Brides and made cameos in Honey West and The Monkees TV series. Sherman left entertainment in the mid-70s, becoming a paramedic and volunteering with the Los Angeles Police Department. He would later become the deputy sheriff of San Bernardino County in California. YouTube: Gigs Rick Davies (Supertramp) Supertramp co-founder, singer and keyboardist Rick Davies died Sept. 6 at the age of 81 after a 10 year battle with Multiple Myeloma.
Davies was the only constant member of Supertramp, which formed in 1970. He also wrote and sang many of their most popular songs, including "Bloody Well Right," "Crime of the Century" and "Goodbye Stranger."
A social media post announcing his passing noted, "His soulful vocals and unmistakable touch on the Wurlitzer became the heartbeat of the bands’ sound.
"Beyond the stage, Rick was known for his warmth, resilience, and devotion to his wife Sue, with whom he shared over five decades. After facing serious health challenges, which kept him unable to continue touring as Supertramp, he enjoyed performing with his hometown buds as Ricky and the Rockets. Rick’s music and legacy continue to inspire many and bears testament to the fact that great songs never die, they live on."
Adam Gasson/Prog Magazine/Future, Getty Images Allen Blickle (ex-Baroness) Former Baroness drummer Allen Blickle died in September at the age of 42.
Blickle was a member of the group dating back to their earliest original lineup and he exited the band in 2013 after he and several other members of the band suffered injuries in a 2012 bus crash.
“It breaks my heart to have to share the news that my dear friend, creative partner and former bandmate Allen Blickle passed away a few days ago. I’m still in shock that he’s gone. We ask for understanding as his family and this band process his passing and grieve his loss. Allen, I love you and miss you. I treasure every moment we shared,” shared Baroness frontman John Baizley through the band's Instagram .
Blickle handled drums on Baroness' Red Album , Blue Record and Yellow & Green album before his exit.
Blickle's credits also included stints with Romantic Dividends, A Place to Bury Strangers and Alpaca. YouTube: Ángel Kêrberos Fredrik Lindgren (Unleashed) Fredrik Lindgren, the original guitarist for death metal titans Unleashed, died on Jan. 5 at the age of 53.
The musician was a part of the group from 1989-1995, appearing on their first four studio albums - 1991's Where No Life Dwells , 1992's Shadows in the Deep , 1993's Across the Open Sea and 1995's Victory .
“Fredrik was a huge part of the early history of the band. For this we are eternally grateful. See you in Valhalla brother! Johnny & The Boys," the group posted in revealing the news on social media .
Lindgren also performed with the groups Terra Firma and Harms Way. YouTube: Rare Metal Videos Ragne Wahlquist (Heavy Load) Ragne Wahlquist, singer and guitarist for the Swedish Viking Metal act Heavy Load, died on Jan. 7 at the age of 69.
Wahlquist founded the band with his brother, drummer Strybjorn Wahlquist, in 1976. He appeared on each of their three early albums - 1978's Full Speed at High Level, 1982's Death or Glory and 1983''s Stronger Than Evil.
The group reunited in 2017 and issued another album, Riders of the Ancient Storm , in 2023. The band was reportedly working on another album with Wahlquist at the time of his death. Chip Somodevilla, Getty Images Peter Yarrow (Peter, Paul & Mary) Peter Yarrow, part of the legendary '60s folk trio Peter, Paul and Mary, died on Jan. 7 at the age of 86.
His death was confirmed by his publicist who revealed that Yarrow had been battling bladder cancer for the last four years.
The trio scored one of their first hits with the Bob Dylan-penned, "Blowin' in the Wind" which reached No. 2 and yielded a pair of Grammy wins for the band. Yarrow sang lead on several Peter, Paul and Mary including "Puff the Magic Dragon" that he also co-wrote.
The trio released nine studio albums between 1962 and 1969, They split in 1970 to pursue solo careers, but did reunite several times over the years to come. Michael Uhll /Redferns, Getty Images P. Fluid (24-7 Spyz) Founding 24-7 Spyz frontman P. Fluid (also known as Peter Forrest) was discovered beaten to death on Jan. 13 in New York City. He was 64.
The musician had been serving as an ambulette driver and his co-workers became concerned after he missed a few stops and hadn't checked in. Upon finding the vehicle, the door window had been broken and Forrest was lying face down in the back of the vehicle.
24-7 Spyz had their greatest success in the late '80s and early '90s delivering a brand of funk metal representative of the different influences that the band had picked up in their native Bronx. They've amassed eight studio albums over the course of their career, with P. Fluid providing vocals on three of them.
He appeared on the 1989 debut Harder Than You and the 1990 follow-up Gumbo Millennium before he bowed out of the band following their 1990 tour with Jane's Addiction. P-Fluid later returned to the band in 1994 and appeared on their fourth studio album in 1995, Temporarily Disconnected . But after a quick tour to support the record, the singer left the group again. Harmony Gerber, Getty Images Toby Myers (John Mellencamp) Toby Myers, the longtime John Mellencamp bassist, died on Jan. 16 at the age of 75.
“Sadness has entered the Mellencamp band and John over the passing of a longtime member,” said a note on Mellencamp’s website . “Toby was a great contribution to the music, and the band. We will miss him as a friend, and a fellow musician.”
Prior to playing with Mellencamp, Myers was a member of Roadmaster, a '70s group that was discovered by Todd Rundgren and released four studio albums.
Myers joined Mellencamp's band in 1982 and appeared on smash albums including Uh-Huh , Scarecrow and The Lonesome Jubilee . He exited the band in 1999 after deciding to become a stay-at-home dad to his newborn son. Jeff Vespa/WireImage, Getty Images Aaron Rossi (Ministry) Aaron Rossi, the former drummer for Ministry , died from a heart attack on Jan. 27 at at the age of 44.
The musician was part of Ministry when they were nominated for a Grammy for "Senor Peligro" in 2010 from their Adios ... Puta Madres live album. He also appeared on the 2013 effort, From Beer to Eternity .
Rossi's credits also include appearances on albums from John 5, Prong and Ankla. Jay West/WireImage, Getty Images Sal Maida (Cracker, Roxy Music, Sparks) Former Cracker bassist Sal Maida died on Feb. 1 at the age of 76 after complications from a fall.
"We had the pleasure of having Sal Maida as a bass player for many years. We made some of our best recordings when he was our bass player. But more than that he was incredible person with a huge heart. We will miss him," noted the band Cracker on social media while recognizing his passing.
Maida's credits in the music industry were plentiful. He had also performed with Roxy Music, Sparks and Milk N' Cookies and provided bass on Cherie Currie's debut solo album.
He joined Cracker in 2006 and co-wrote on their 2009 album Sunrise in the Land of Milk and Honey . Michael Putland, Getty Images Jamie Muir (King Crimson) Former King Crimson percussionist Jamie Muir died on Feb. 17 at the age of 79.
Muir had a brief stint in the band after starting his career with The Music Improvisation Company, Boris and Assagai. It was in 1972 that he received the call to join what would be a new incarnation of King Crimson. He appeared on the 1973 album, Larks' Tongues in Aspic .
Shortly after the release of the album, Muir left the band and pursued a monastic lifestyle in Southern Scotland while adhering to strict principles of Buddhism.
He would later return to the music business in 1980, but gave it up for good in 1990 when he turned his focus to painting. BSR Agency/Gentle Look, Getty Images Rick Buckler (The Jam) Rick Buckler, best known for his time as the drummer for British alt-rock trio The Jam, died on Feb. 17 at the age of 69.
The band issued six albums between 1977 and 1982, amassing their greatest success in the U.K. Among their biggest hits were "A Town Called Malice," "That's Entertainment," "Start!," "Absolute Beginners" and "Beat Surrender."
After The Jam, Buckler formed Time UK and later reunited with bassist Bruce Foxton in the band Sharp. Outside of his music career, Buckler also worked in production and music management as well as spending time as a carpenter and an artist. YouTube: Roadrunner Records Coburn Pharr (Annihilator) On Feb. 25, it was revealed that former Anihilator singer Coburn Pharr had died at the age of 62.
Longtime Annihilator member Jeff Waters shared news of the death on social media , commenting, "Coburn was the singer on our best and biggest record. He had the most unique voice of all our singers, along with Randy Rampage (he also passed, in 2018)."
According to Waters, he had last reconnected with Coburn in 2018 and the singer had previously joined them in 2015 on the 70,000 Tons of Metal Cruise.
The singer was best known for his work on the Never, Neverland album. Michael Putland, Getty Images Joey Molland (Badfinger) Joey Molland, guitarist for the '70s superstars Badfinger, died on March 1 at the age of 77.
His music career started with the group Gary Walker and the Rain before he moved on to join The Iveys that were part of The Beatles' Apple Records label. The group eventually changed their name to Badfinger and began what proved to be a successful run from the late 1960s into the 1970s.
Molland played on seven Badfinger albums, with songs such as "No Matter What," "Day By Day" and 'Baby Blue" becoming rock radio staples.
Outside of Badfinger, Molland appeared on George Harrison's All Things Must Pass album and The Concert for Bangladesh album as well as John Lennon's Imagine .
Following Badfinger's split, Molland formed the band Natural Gas who released one album. He also issued six solo records while also partaking in various Badfinger reunions. YouTube: CrackerVEVO Bob Rupe (Cracker) Bob Rupe, the bassist for Cracker in the mid- '90s, died on March 3 at the age of 68.
The bassist first appeared on Cracker's 1996 album, The Golden Age and later appeared on the 1998 album Gentleman's Blues before exiting the group in early 2000.
"Bob was the charismatic and talented bassist for Cracker from roughly 1994 to 1999. Along with the late Charlie Quintana, he formed the rhythm section that powered Cracker’s theatre and shed tours at the peak of the band's popularity," noted the band in recognizing Rupe's death .
Outside of Cracker, Rupe was a founding member of The Silos and had also played with Gutterball, House of Freaks and Sparklehorse. Ian Dickson/Redferns, Getty Images Brian James (The Damned) Brian James, the founding guitarist and songwriter for The Damned and a onetime member of Lords of the New Church, died on March 6 at the age of 70.
After starting his career in the early '70s with the garage rock band Bastard, James joined the proto-punk band London SS before eventually finding success with The Damned. He wrote a majority of the material on their first two albums - Damned Damned Damned and Music for Pleasure - before deciding to leave the group in 1977.
James would later toil in Tanz Der Youth and as a member of Iggy Pop's touring band before finding his second shot of success with The Lords of the New Church. Other future bands included The Dripping Lips and The Racketeers.
James also issued five solo albums and one solo EP. Ed Perlstein, Getty Images Jesse Colin Young (The Youngbloods) Jesse Colin Young, the singer-songwriter for The Youngbloods, died on March 16 at the age of 83.
The band's biggest song was their cover of Chet Powers' "Get Together." The group issued five studio albums before their split in 1972.
After the band members went their separate ways, Young embarked on a solo career. In total, he issued 17 solo records. Michael Tran/FilmMagic, Getty Images Marty Callner Marty Callner, the acclaimed music video director, died on March 17 from natural causes at his home in Malibu, Calif., at the age of 78.
Callner directed some of the '80s most classic videos including Twisted Sister's "We're Not Gonna Take It" and "I Wanna Rock," Whitesnake's "Here I Go Again" and "Is This Love?," Poison's "Every Rose Has Its Thorn" and Aerosmith's "Livin' on the Edge," "Dude Looks Like a Lady" and "Love in an Elevator."
He would expand his reach to include concert specials, comedy videos for Jerry Seinfeld, Dane Cook and Robin Williams and toward the end of his career he created the sports documentary series Hard Knocks . Frazer Harrison, Getty Images Dave Allen (Gang of Four) Dave Allen, the founding bassist for Gang of Four , died on March 10 at the age of 68.
Allen was among the band's original members when they formed in 1976 in Leeds. Their debut album, Entertainment! , arrived in 1979 and kicked off what would be a successful career.
The bassist would split from the band shortly after 1981's Solid Gold album and found his next musical adventure playing with XTC's Barry Andrews in the band Shreikback. His resume also includes stints with Elastic Purejoy and Low Pop Suicide.
Outside of his bands, Allen went on to form the World Domination Recordings music label, while also working for Intel and Apple Music at different times in his life.
Glen E. Friedman Al Barile (SSD) Al Barile, the founding guitarist for first wave hardcore vets SSD, died on April 6 at the age of 63 after a battle with cancer.
As a member of SSD, Barile helped launch their career with 1982's The Kids Will Have Their Say and 1983's Get It Away EP. The band would split after 1985's Break It Up , but Barile would once again surface in the '90s with the alt-rock outfit Gage.
Gie Knaeps, Getty Images David Thomas (Pere Ubu) Longtime Pere Ubu frontman David Thomas died April 23 following a "long illness" at the age of 71.
Pere Ubu formed in Cleveland in 1975 and Thomas was the lone member of the group to remain through its existence. Over the course of their history, the band recorded 19 studio albums and were said to be in the process of recording their 20th. An official statement revealed the group's intent to finish mixing the record and eventually release it.
The band's style shifted with the decades, infusing elements of proto-punk, new wave, industrial rock and art rock into their sound. Though they had little commercial success, they remained a presence on college rock radio and underground music stations. Frazer Harrison, Getty Images Jill Sobule Singer/songriter Jill Sobule, best known for her alt-rock '90s hits "I Kissed a Girl" and "Supermodel," died in a house fire on May 1 at the age of 66. The musician was staying with a friend in St. Paul, Minnesota when the fire occurred.
Sobule issued 12 studio albums over a three-decade career. In addition to her own work, the singer-songwriter was also known for the theme song to Nickelodeon's Unfabulous . YouTube: Summer of Phil James Baker (Hoodoo Gurus) James Baker, best known as the drummer for Aussie college rock favorites Hoodoo Gurus, died on May 5 at the age of 71.
In addition to Hoodoo Gurus, Baker performed with such acts as The Scientists, The Beasts of Bourbon and The Victims.
Baker was a founding member of the Hoodoo Gurus and appeared on their 1984 debut Stoneage Romance before exiting the band. Paul Natkin, Getty Images Chris Hager (Mickey Ratt, Rough Cutt) Former Mickey Ratt and Rough Cutt guitarist Chris Hager died May 19 at the age of 67.

YouTube - IFM RAW Adam Lee Ramey Dropout Kings vocalist Adam Lee Ramey died on May 19 at the age of 32.
According to a post on the band's socials , "With the heaviest hearts, we share that our brother, Adam Ramey has passed away. His passion, energy, and love for music shaped Dropout Kings and touched countless lives. We’re devastated to say the least, but Adam’s spirit, charisma and energy will not only forever inspire us, but will push us into the future to be the best that we can. We appreciate you all during this time and know he absolutely did as well for all the times we’ve shared."
After the breakup of his previous band The Bad Chapter in 2015, Ramey formed a group called Phoenix Down with some of his former bandmates and rapper Eddie Wellz. They changed their name to Dropout Kings in 2017, and by that point the lineup also consisted of Staig Flynn, Chucky Guzman, Rob Sebastian and Trevor Norgren. Big Picture Media Dave Shapiro Music industry veteran and Sound Talent Group co-founder Dave Shapiro was killed in a California plane crash on May 22.
Shapiro, who also owned Velocity Records, was an ardent supporter of rock and metal, with the Sound Talent Group roster including artists such as Pierce the Veil, Lamb of God, I Prevail, Sum 41, Beartooth, Movements, Ice Nine Kills, Killswitch Engage, Motionless In White, In This Moment, Parkway Drive, Black Label Society and many more. Chelsea Lauren, Getty Images Daniel Williams (formerly The Devil Wears Prada) Former The Devil Wears Prada drummer Daniel Williams died in a San Diego plane crash on May 22, along with Sound Talent Group and Velocity Records owner Dave Shapiro. Williams played with The Devil Wears Prada from their inception in 2005 until 2016.
In the wake of Williams' death, TDWP paid tribute to him and Williams with an Instagram post that said, "No words. We owe you everything. Love you forever." Ian Dickson/Redferns, Getty Images James Lowe (The Electric Prunes) James Lowe, the lead singer of the '60s psychedelic rock outfit The Electric Prunes, died on May 22 at the age of 82.
As a member of The Electric Prunes, he released five studio albums under its initial incarnation. After the band split, he retained the rights to the name and reactivated the band for future recordings starting in the 2000s. The band's biggest hits were "I Had Too Much to Dream (Last Night)" and "Get Me to the World On Time."
In later years, Lowe also achieved success as a recording engineer working closely with Todd Rundgren's band Nazz. He also produced and directed commercials and children's shows for Disney. Jimi Celeste, Getty Images Ananda Lewis Former MTV and BET VJ Ananda Lewis died at the age of 52 on June 11.
Lewis was the host of several MTV shows during her stint with the network. She initially appeared on MTV Live before it became Total Request Live ( TRL ) as well as 12 Angry Viewers, Hot Zone and MTV Jams .
Jim Dyson, Getty Images Douglas McCarthy (Nitzer Ebb) Nitzer Ebb vocalist Douglas McCarthy died on June 11 at the age of 58.
McCarthy formed the band with drummer Dave Gooday and keyboardist Bon Harris in 1982. Their first album, That Total Age , arrived in 1987 and they became one of the leading acts in the '80s industrial rock scene.
They would issue five albums before they split in 1995. But the band would reunite in 2006 and later issued their first album since reuniting in 2010 with Industrial Complex . Adrenaline PR Chuck Profus (Agent Steel / Obscene Gesture) Chuck Profus, drummer for speed and thrash metal bands Agent Steel and Obscene Gesture, died on June 4 in Los Angeles at the age of 61.
Profus fulfilled his dream of being a pro when he co-founded Agent Steel with John Cyriis in 1983. Their first show was opening for Slayer on the opening date of Haunting The Chapel launch at the world-famous Country Club in Reseda. With the entire Metal music industry present the band bulldozed through a 30-minute set of classics like “Taken By Force”, “Agents of Steel”, “Bleed for the Godz” and “144,000 Gone” and everyone understood the band was the next big thing in the era of Metallica, Megadeth, Slayer, Exodus and Anthrax.
After his exit from the band in 2002, Profus founded his punk metal alter ego band Obscene Gesture with original Agent Steel bassist George Robb. He had suffered some physical setbacks through injury, and he was just having fun again. The band recorded two albums. Chris Jackson, Getty Images Patrick Walden (Babyshambles) Patrick Walden, the former guitarist of 2000s-era Brit rock band Babyshambles, died on June 20 at the age of 46.
Walden had played with the groups Fluid, The White Sport and Six Cold Thousand before landing the gig with Pete Doherty's post-Libertines band, Babyshambles. He co-wrote several songs on the band's debut album, but exited the band temporarily in 2006 after a domestic dispute before returning to the group from 2007-2009 after a charge against him was dropped. Though he played with the group on occasion during that period, he was never officially renamed a member over that time.
"We feel very fortunate to have known, loved and worked with him," said a message shared by Babyshambles after Walden's passing.

YouTube: Aftershocks TV Tim Cronin (Monster Magnet) Founding Monster Magnet member Tim Cronin died in July at the age of 63 after being diagnosed with ALS earlier in the year.
Cronin started as the band's drummer in 1989 before moving over to play bass. He appeared on their 1990 and 1991 EPs, as well as their 1991 debut album Spine of God . He's also credited on their 1993 album Superjudge though he had exited the band prior to its release.
Cronin had also served as lead singer for the band Ribeye Brothers. And later in life, he manned the counter at Red Bank, New Jersey's Jack's Music Shoppe.
Kevin Nixon/Metal Hammer Magazine/Future, Getty Images Matt Keil (Comeback Kid) Matt Keil, the former Comeback Kid bassist, has died after a battle with ALS.
The band issued a statement , noting, "He was such an amazing friend and musician. Just the greatest guy to tour with, be around, and explore the world with."
Keil played in Comeback Kid between 2008 and 2014. He appeared on their albums Symptoms + Cures and Die Knowing .

Kooymans was a co-founding member of the band who continued to perform with the group until 2021 when he was diagnosed with ALS.
"We say goodbye to a great musician and composer whose work extended beyond Golden Earring," reads the short statement released to the press via Kooyman's family. "George was a beloved husband, father, grandfather, but above all, a friend."

YouTube: JunkyardVEVO David Roach (Junkyard) David Roach, lead singer for veteran rockers Junkyard, died at his home on Aug. 2 after a battle with squamous cell carcinoma at the age of 62.
The singer had been part of the band's early days, joining in 1987.

Ian Dickson/Redferns, Getty Images Terry Reid Terry Reid, the British singer who turned down both Led Zeppelin and Deep Purple, died on Aug. 4 at the age of 75.
Reid began performing in British clubs in the early '60s, when the band he was in, Peter Jay and the Jaywalkers, opened for the Rolling Stones .
By the end of the decade, he was tapped by the Stones as a solo artist to open some of their most high-profile shows. During this era, Reid, known as Superlungs for his powerful voice, also opened for Cream , Fleetwood Mac, and Jethro Tull .
In 1968, as Jimmy Page was assembling the New Yardbirds out of the previous band that had recently lost singer Keith Relf, he asked Reid to join the group, which would soon be renamed Led Zeppelin.
Reid, on the road with the Rolling Stones at the time, told Page he didn't want to leave the Stones and upcoming Cream tours he was on, but offered to try out some things with the new band if the guitarist wanted to talk to Keith Richards about the situation.
Instead, Reid suggested to Page that he check out a group called Band of Joy, which recently supported Reid on tour, and particularly their singer, Robert Plant , and drummer, John Bonham , both of whom would soon join Led Zeppelin.
Soon after, guitarist Ritchie Blackmore invited Reid to join Deep Purple after their original singer, Rod Evans, left. Reid turned down his offer, preferring to focus on his solo career. Ian Gillan took the job.
Reid released more than a half-dozen solo albums, starting with 1968's Bang, Bang You're Terry Reid . His most acclaimed record, 1973's River , was reexamined in 2016, when previously unreleased recordings from the sessions were issued as The Other Side of the River .
By the early 1980s, Reid became a full-time session vocalist, collaborating with artists such as Don Henley , Bonnie Raitt, and the Replacements .
Michael Ochs Archives, Getty Images Bobby Whitlock (Derek and the Dominos) Bobby Whitlock (pictured second in from left), organ player and co-founder of Derek and the Dominos, died on Aug. 10 at the age of 77.
Whitlock's career began in the mid-'60s when he signed to Stax Records and quickly garnered a reputation for his piano and organ playing. That led him to appearing on recordings from Booker T. and the MG's and Sam & Dave.
He would later team up with Eric Clapton in Delaney and Bonnie and Friends in 1968 before that would work together again on 1970's Layla and Other Assorted Love Songs under the moniker Derek and the Dominos. The group lasted for one album before splitting in 1971.
Whitlock also appeared on George Harrison's All Things Must Pass in 1970 and eventually issued a handful of solo records before taking a hiatus from the music industry in the mid-'70s. He didn't return to recording until 1999, but issued nine more albums after his eventual comeback.
YouTube: The Ed Sullivan Show Mark Volman (The Turtles) Mark Volman, a co-founding member of The Turtles who played guitar, keyboards, tambourine and added backing vocals, died on Sept. 5 at the age of 78.
The musician appeared on five albums with the legendary '60s band, who yielded such smash hits as "Happy Together" and "You Showed Me."
He was later a member of Flo & Eddie and spent time as a member of Frank Zappa's The Mothers of Invention in the '70s. Bruce Loose (Flipper) Bruce "Loose" Calderwood, frontman and bassist for the punk vets Flipper, died on Sept. 4 at the age of 66. The band confirmed in a social media posting that Bruce died after suffering a heart attack.
The singer appeared on all four of the band's albums. Though mainstream success would not come, the group is said to have been heavily influential on such acts as Nirvana and Melvins.
